title_original: The Vermeer Obsessive Who Changed Art History
excerpt_original: Vermeer has one man to thank for catapulting him into the limelight almost 200 years after his death.

blocks.text: If you were asked to identify Johannes Vermeer , you might answer that he is one of the world’s most famous Old Masters, that his Girl with the Pearl Earring (ca. 1665) is perhaps the pinnacle of the Dutch Golden Age, or that he was one of the Netherlands’s greatest-ever artists.

But if you were to ask the same question to someone in 1800, the answer would likely be “who?”

While his mammoth reputation today would suggest otherwise, for the 200 years following his death, Vermeer was largely forgotten. His unlikely return to the spotlight was thanks to a single French art critic. But why did he disappear?

When Vermeer died aged just 43 in 1675, he was in debt and had mostly fallen into obscurity outside of his hometown of Delft in the Dutch Republic. Only 34 paintings are firmly accepted to have been painted by Vermeer, as he worked slowly and fastidiously. He didn’t work in a large studio, leaving no pupils behind who were dedicated to the continuation of his style after his death. He rarely travelled, and so had not built a reputation in major cities. His widow was forced to sell most of his works to pay off their debts, spreading his work across the country. All of these factors stunted the development of Vermeer’s legacy.

By the mid-19th century, Vermeer was of such little repute that works by him were sometimes forged with a signature by Pieter de Hooch —an artist whose name carried significantly more weight at the time—to increase their prices. So how did he re-enter the spotlight?

links.text: forged with a signature by Pieter de Hooch

blocks.text: Johannes Vermeer, View of Delft (ca. 1660–61). Photo: Buyenlarge/Getty Images.

Etienne-Joseph-Théophile Thoré was a French art critic and collector living in exile across Western Europe from 1849–1859 due to his support of French Revolutionary radicals. During that time, he wrote under the pseudonym W. Bürger . He had first seen Vermeer’s work, View of Delft (ca. 1660–61) in 1842 and was bowled over, but found locating more work by Vermeer so impossible that he referred to the artist as his “sphinx,” the riddle-providing creature of Greek mythology. As he travelled through Europe he began to collect paintings he believed could have been by the enigmatic artist.

In 1866, an exhibition of Old Master paintings was held at the Palais des Champs-Élysées and Thoré-Bürger contributed six Vermeer works to the show. Five additional paintings attributed to Vermeer were also displayed, although several were later reattributed to Vermeer’s contemporaries. Nonetheless, thanks to the exhibition and two articles Thoré-Bürger published about the artist, in addition to a catalogue of his works, Vermeer was back in the art world.

blocks.alt: a painting of a woman in profile turning to look at us, she has her hair pulled back in a wrapped cloth that is blue and yellow and she is wearing a large pearl earring

blocks.text: Johannes Vermeer, Girl with a Pearl Earring (ca. 1665). Photo: Sepia Times/ Universal Images Group via Getty Images.

The market took its time to catch up with Vermeer’s mounting legacy, however, and when Girl with a Pearl Earring came to auction in 1881 it sold for just two guilders and 30 cents—the equivalent of $35 . Today, estimates for the painting’s value reach $600 million.

After his death, a number of Thoré-Bürger’s Vermeer paintings were sold. Three of them are now held in public collections: A Young Woman Standing at a Virginal (ca. 1670–72) and A Young Woman Seated at the Virginal (ca. 1670–72) are at London’s National Gallery ; and Young Woman with a Pearl Necklace (ca. 1664) is held at Berlin’s Gemäldegalerie . Meanwhile, The Concert (1664), one of 13 works stolen from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in 1990, is considered the most valuable missing piece of art in the world, valued at $200 million.

links.text: most valuable missing piece of art

blocks.text: Another painting— A Young Woman Seated at the Virginals , long in a private Belgian collection—resurfaced at Sotheby’s London in 2004, selling for $30.1 million to casino magnate Steve Wynn . It was the first Vermeer to appear at public auction in over 80 years and remains his auction record.
Despite there being fewer than 40 known paintings attributed to him, thanks to Thoré-Bürger’s dogged pursuit of his sphinx, Vermeer isn’t going anywhere.
